subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 10 periods = 400 minutes
Total: 10 periods · 6h 40min

section_titles: Fun at Vegetable Market — comparing weights
periods.activity_title: Heavier, Lighter — Reading Weight from Lived Experience

tasks_in_class.description: Look at pictures of animals and write their names from heaviest to lightest.
Write the name of the heaviest object in your home and explain how you know.
What do you think will be the weight of the half pumpkin? Write your estimate.

time_bands.activity: Students look at the vegetable market picture on p.115 and share what they notice about how the seller is weighing vegetables. A quick round gathers what unit or method students think is being used, drawing on their own experience of markets and kitchens.

Opening Q1, p.115 ("Look at pictures of animals and write their...."). Students write the animals in order from heaviest to lightest individually, then pairs compare their ordering and discuss disagreements — focusing on the reasoning, not just the answer.

Opening Q2, p.115 ("Write the name of the heaviest object in your...."). Students write their response and share with a partner, articulating how they know — by lifting, by comparing with another object, or by reading a label. The class pools a few examples.

Fun at Vegetable Market, p.115 ("What do you think will be the weight of the...."). Students write their estimate of the half-pumpkin's weight and briefly explain their thinking. A few estimates are shared aloud; the class notices whether different strategies give similar ranges.

periods.teacher_notes: Opening Q3, Q4, and Q5 (p.115) cover the same kind of lived-weight reasoning as Q2 and Q6 — students reflecting on their own experience of effort and personal weight. These make good paired or individual follow-up: note them in your copy as additional practice for students who finish early or as a home conversation starter. A common slip at this stage is treating heaviness as the same as bigness — prompt students to think of a small stone and a large balloon as a counterexample.

section_titles: Kilograms and grams — fractions of a kilogram
periods.activity_title: Packing Packets — Half, Quarter, and Tenth of a Kilogram

tasks_in_class.description: Estimate the weight of 6 bananas, 5 potatoes, 10 tomatoes, 15 onions as less/more than 1 kg; verify using a weighing balance.
Look at pictures: 2×500g=1kg so 500g=½kg; 4×250g=1kg so 250g=¼kg; 10×100g=1kg. Try doing the same with actual packets.

time_bands.activity: Let Us Do, p.116 ("Estimate the weight of 6 bananas, 5 potatoes, 10 tomatoes...."). Students predict each — less than or more than 1 kg — and record. If a balance is available, small groups verify; if not, the teacher shares actual weights for discussion. Students revisit any estimates that surprised them.

Let Us Explore Q1 (a)(b)(c), p.116–117 ("Look at pictures: 2×500g=1kg so 500g=½kg...."). Students study the three pan-balance pictures in order: two 500 g packets, then four 250 g packets, then ten 100 g packets, each time seeing what balances 1 kg. They record the fraction relationship each picture reveals before moving to the next.

Students use the three relationships just discovered (500 g = ½ kg, 250 g = ¼ kg, 100 g = 1/10 kg) to check their earlier produce estimates — was 6 bananas more or less than ½ kg? A brief whole-class discussion connects the pictorial evidence to the fraction names.

periods.teacher_notes: The pan-balance pictures are the primary evidence for each fraction; students should articulate in words why two 500 g packets balance 1 kg before writing '½'. A frequent error is confusing ¼ kg with 400 g — pressing students to say 'four equal parts make one whole' before writing the fraction helps. If actual packets (sand-filled bags or labelled containers) are available, even one demonstration with physical objects greatly deepens the pictorial work.
materials: Sand-filled or labelled 500 g, 250 g, 100 g packets (if available)
Produce or pictures of bananas, potatoes, tomatoes, onions

section_titles: Comparing weights — pan balance and unit matching
periods.activity_title: Tipping the Balance — Drawing, Predicting, and Matching

tasks_in_class.description: How many 250 g packets balance one 500 g packet? Draw packets on the empty pan; complete: 250 g = ___ of 500 g.
Draw arrows to indicate which side the pan balance will tilt for each of the four pictures (a–d).
Match objects (baby, eraser, pen, books, table, fridge, etc.) to the units kilogram or grams.

time_bands.activity: Let Us Find Q1, p.117 ("How many 250 g packets balance one 500 g packet? Draw...."). Students draw packets on the blank pan and then complete the fraction statement. They share their drawings with a neighbour and check that both pans would balance.

Let Us Find Q2, p.118 ("Draw arrows to indicate which side the pan balance will tilt...."). Students work through all four pictures (a–d), predicting the tilt before drawing the arrow. After each prediction, a partner checks and the pair resolves any disagreement by reasoning about which side has more grams.

Let Us Find Q3, p.118 ("Match objects — baby, eraser, pen, books, table, fridge — to...."). Students match each object to kg or g individually, then the class discusses any items where there was disagreement — focusing on what made the choice obvious or uncertain.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently place large or familiar objects in the wrong unit column — a gas cylinder in 'grams', for example — because they associate 'big' with 'kilo' and ignore the actual mass involved. Use one clear anchor: an eraser weighs about 10 g, a textbook about 300 g, a full school bag about 3–5 kg. Let Us Do Q1–Q3 (p.119) and Let Us Think Q1–Q4 (p.119) extend the eraser-and-fraction reasoning further and work well as consolidation tasks; note them for students who finish the matching activity early.
materials: An actual eraser (to demonstrate its weight by feel)

section_titles: Comparing weights — pan balance and unit matching
periods.activity_title: Erasers as a Unit — Solving Sweet-Box Packing Problems

tasks_in_class.description: How many erasers (each 10 g) will weigh the same as a 50 g Haldi packet?

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Think Q1–Q4 (Boxes of Sweet), p.119
tasks_in_class.description: How many boxes of 500 g, 250 g, 100 g, and 50 g each are needed to pack 1 kg Kaju-katli? Write the number for each customer.

homework.description: A 100 g soap bar will weigh the same as _______ erasers (each 10 g).
_______ erasers will weigh the same as 250 g sugar.

time_bands.activity: The class revisits the eraser as a unit: each eraser weighs 10 g, just as was established when comparing objects to units. Let Us Do Q1, p.119 ("How many erasers, each 10 g, will weigh the same as a 50 g Haldi....") is solved individually, with students writing how they counted up by tens.

Let Us Think Q1–Q4 (Boxes of Sweet), p.119 ("How many boxes of 500 g, 250 g, 100 g, and 50 g each are needed...."). Students work through each customer's order, connecting the box size to the fraction relationships built in the kilograms and grams unit — a 500 g box is half a kilogram, so two of them fill an order. Groups share their reasoning for each box size.

A brief class discussion asks: which customer's order needs the most boxes, and why? Students articulate that smaller sub-units require more boxes to reach 1 kg. Let Us Do Q2 and Q3 (p.119) are set as paired take-home work to extend the eraser-unit reasoning.

periods.teacher_notes: The eraser tasks (Q1–Q3, p.119) are the bridge between the fraction relationships and the multiplication/division logic — students who understand '10 g × 5 = 50 g' are ready for the sweet-box reasoning. A common error in the Boxes of Sweet task is giving the answer as the fraction rather than the count (writing ½ instead of 2 boxes); prompt with 'how many boxes does the customer carry home?'. Let Us Do Q2 and Q3 are set as homework as they repeat the same eraser-counting procedure with larger gram targets.

section_titles: Weighing machines and real-life weight estimation
periods.activity_title: Lift, Estimate, Match — Weighing Machines in Real Life

tasks_in_class.description: Lift objects around you; write names of three you can lift easily and estimate their weights.
Write names of things you can lift with a lot of effort; estimate and write their weights.
Match objects (cat, elephant, 1-litre bottle, tiger, gas cylinder, pen, leaf, wooden chair) with estimated weight ranges.

time_bands.activity: The teacher briefly presents the pictures of different weighing machines on p.120 — pan balance, baby scale, kitchen scale, bathroom scale, luggage scale — and students name where they have seen each one. The class connects each machine type to the kind of object it is used for, building the vocabulary 'weighing machine' alongside the concept of choosing the right tool.

Let Us Do Q1 and Q2, p.121 ("Lift objects around you; write names of three you can lift easily...."; "Write names of things you can lift with a lot of effort...."). Students physically lift classroom objects, record the easy ones and the effortful ones in two columns, and write an estimated weight for each. Pairs compare their lists and discuss disagreements about which column an item belongs in.

Let Us Do Q4, p.121 ("Match objects — cat, elephant, 1-litre bottle, tiger, gas cylinder, pen, leaf, wooden chair — with estimated weight ranges."). Students complete the matching individually. The class then discusses two or three items where the match was tricky — for example, distinguishing the weight of a gas cylinder from a wooden chair — using the anchor values from lifting experience.

periods.teacher_notes: Let Us Do (monthly consumption table), p.120, and Let Us Do Q3 (a–d), p.121, involve data gathering at home and multi-packet counting; both work well as take-home investigations rather than in-class tasks — note them for students to try with family. A common error in the matching task is using size as a proxy for weight; prompt students to recall what they just lifted: a heavy book is small, a large cardboard box may be light.
materials: Classroom objects of varied weights — books, pencil box, bag, water bottle, chalk box

section_titles: Weighing machines and real-life weight estimation
periods.activity_title: From Kilograms to Packets — Solving Real-Life Weight Problems

tasks_in_class.description: How many 1 kg packets are in 10 kg, 20 kg, 50 kg, and 25 kg? Write the answers.

time_bands.activity: Students hold or look at a 1 kg object (a full water bottle, a book bag with one book) and agree: that is roughly 1 kg. The teacher asks how many such objects would be needed to make 10 kg — students count in tens on their fingers or on a number line drawn on the board.

Let Us Do Q3 (a–d), p.121 ("How many 1 kg packets are in 10 kg, 20 kg, 50 kg, and 25 kg?"). Students solve all four parts in their notebooks, showing how they reached each answer — whether by repeated addition, counting in tens, or a direct statement. Groups then compare strategies.

A short class discussion invites students to pose their own similar question: 'If one packet weighs 1 kg, how many do I need for _____ kg?' Students exchange questions with a partner and solve each other's. The teacher highlights that these are the same bags seen on grocery shelves and at ration shops, connecting the mathematics to real supply contexts.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit extends the kilogram reasoning into multiplication territory; students who are fluent in counting by tens will complete Q3 quickly, so the question-posing extension at the end is essential for keeping the unit substantive. A frequent error is reversing the question — writing the number of kilograms in one packet rather than the number of packets in the bulk quantity; restating 'how many packets fit into the big bag?' as a concrete image helps. Let Us Do (monthly consumption table), p.120, asking students to survey home quantities of atta, rice, pulses, and sugar, fits naturally as a home investigation following this unit.
materials: A 1-litre water bottle or similarly weighted object as a 1 kg proxy

section_titles: Measuring capacity — litre, millilitre, and fractions
periods.activity_title: Containers and Fractions — Filling a Litre with Smaller Bottles

tasks_in_class.description: Find bottles/containers that hold less than 1 litre, exactly 1 litre, and more than 1 litre; write their names in the table.
How many 500 ml, 250 ml, 100 ml bottles fill a 1 l bottle? How many 250 ml in ½ l and 750 ml? How many 100 ml in ½ l and 800 ml?

time_bands.activity: Measuring Capacity (containers table), p.122 ("Find bottles and containers that hold less than 1 litre, exactly 1 litre, and more than 1 litre...."). Students examine the classroom collection of containers or think of containers they know from home, classify them into three columns, and write names. The class shares and agrees on a common list, sorting any disputed containers by reasoning about relative size.

Let Us Find (a)(b)(c)(d), p.123–124 ("How many 500 ml, 250 ml, 100 ml bottles fill a 1 l bottle? How many 250 ml in ½ l...."). Students work through each sub-question in order, first predicting the answer and then checking with the pouring activity or the pictorial evidence in the book. Each relationship — 2×500 ml = 1 l, 4×250 ml = 1 l, 10×100 ml = 1 l — is written as a sentence and as a fraction. The parallel to the kilogram fraction work is drawn aloud: the structure is the same, only the attribute changes.

periods.teacher_notes: The capacity fraction relationships (500 ml = ½ l, 250 ml = ¼ l, 100 ml = 1/10 l) mirror exactly the kilogram relationships students have already reasoned through; name those earlier relationships aloud so students can transfer the logic rather than treating capacity as brand new. If containers and water are available, even a quick physical pour for the first sub-question anchors the pictorial evidence powerfully. A common slip is writing '½ litre = 250 ml' by confusing the quarter and half relationships — having students check by doubling ('if ½ litre were 250 ml, a full litre would be only 500 ml — is that right?') catches the error quickly.
materials: Assorted containers from home or classroom (water bottle, glass, mug, small jar)
Water and a 1-litre bottle (if available for pouring activity)

section_titles: Measuring capacity — litre, millilitre, and fractions
periods.activity_title: Droppers, Dosing Cups, and Packing Perfumed Oil

tasks_in_class.description: Find out how much of these liquids are used at a time: eye drops, honey, cough syrup, cooking oil, and one more.
Mr Krishna has 1 l perfumed oil; how many bottles of 500 ml, 200 ml, 100 ml, and 50 ml does each customer get?

homework.description: Estimate and verify by measuring the capacity of: water bottle, glass, mug, jug, bucket, teaspoon, bowl.

time_bands.activity: Let Us Do Q3 (a–e), p.124 ("Find out how much of these liquids are used at a time: eye drops, honey, cough syrup...."). Students think about or look at label information for each liquid and write how much is used in one dose or one serving. A class discussion asks: which liquid uses the fewest millilitres at a time, and which uses the most? Students order the liquids from smallest to largest serving.

Let Us Do Q4 (a–d), p.125 ("Mr Krishna has 1 l perfumed oil; how many bottles of 500 ml, 200 ml, 100 ml, and 50 ml does each customer get?"). Students solve each sub-question, applying the fraction relationships and the counting-up strategy. The class compares this packing problem to the Kaju-katli sweet-box problem: the structure is identical — how many smaller containers fill a fixed total.

Let Us Do Q5, p.125, and Let Us Explore, p.125, are introduced briefly: students are asked to pick any three containers at home and estimate their capacity before measuring. Let Us Do Q5 is set as a home task. Let Us Do Q1 (a–c, p.124, dosing-cup) and Q2 (a–b, p.124, dropper) are noted as further measuring activities that work well with any medicine cup or dropper available at home.

periods.teacher_notes: Let Us Do Q1 and Q2 (p.124), using a 10 ml dosing cup and a 1 ml dropper, are genuinely hands-on measuring activities; they are noted here as take-home tasks because a medicine cup or dropper is common in most households and the measuring is best done at leisure. The perfumed oil problem (Q4) frequently produces errors for the 200 ml bottle because 1000 ÷ 200 = 5 is not one of the standard fraction relationships — prompt students to count up: 200, 400, 600, 800, 1000. Let Us Explore (p.125, shop visit) works best as a family outing activity noted for home.
materials: Empty bottles or containers with ml markings (if available)
Medicine labels showing dosage in ml (optional, for Q3 context)

section_titles: Water use, conservation, and measuring containers
periods.activity_title: How Much Water? — Comparing and Reasoning About Daily Use

tasks_in_class.description: How many litres of water do you drink daily? How much can a crow drink? How much milk do you drink? How much does an elephant drink?
How much water is used in: shower, watering crops, watering plants, washing clothes, and two more activities? Fill the table using given quantities.

time_bands.activity: Let Us Find (a–d), p.126 ("How many litres of water do you drink daily? How much can a crow drink?...."). Students first write their own estimate for how many litres they drink, then answer the four questions, comparing human to animal quantities. Pairs discuss: which comparison is most surprising — a crow's tiny sip or an elephant's enormous daily intake — and use the ml/litre relationships they have built to place each quantity on a mental scale.

Let Us Find (activities table), p.126 ("How much water is used in: shower, watering crops, watering plants, washing clothes...."). Students fill in the table using the given quantities in the book, then discuss which activity uses the most water and which the least. The class examines whether the quantities feel large or small — connecting them to the litre benchmarks they know from the capacity unit (a 1-litre bottle, a 500 ml glass).

periods.teacher_notes: This unit builds directly on the litre and millilitre relationships from the capacity section — framing large quantities (a shower uses about 60 litres) against the familiar 1-litre bottle helps students make sense of numbers that otherwise feel abstract. A common error is confusing the per-use quantity with a daily total; ask 'is this how much for one time or for the whole day?' to prompt careful reading. The standard milk-measuring can markings (50 ml to 1000 ml) on p.126 can be pointed out as a real-world measuring tool students may recognise from morning milk at home.
materials: A 1-litre water bottle (as a concrete reference for large quantities)

section_titles: Water use, conservation, and measuring containers
periods.activity_title: Drip by Drip — Measuring Water Loss and Thinking About Conservation

tasks_in_class.description: Put a container under a leaking tap for one hour; measure how much water is lost; calculate loss in a day and a week.

time_bands.activity: The class discusses: what happens when a tap drips? Students estimate how much water a slowly dripping tap might lose — a few drops, a few ml, more? They write a personal estimate in their notebooks and share with a partner. The teacher introduces the activity on p.127 and asks what container and measuring tool would be needed to carry it out.

Water Conservation activity, p.127 ("Put a container under a leaking tap for one hour; measure how much water is lost...."). Where the school permits it, a dripping tap or a tap opened to a slow drip is set up; students place a container beneath it for a timed interval, then measure the collected water using a marked container. Where a live tap is not accessible, the teacher provides a sample reading (e.g. 120 ml in one hour) and students work from that number.

Students calculate how much water the dripping tap would waste in a full day (24 hours) and in a week (7 days), using repeated addition or multiplication. Results are shared and compared — students notice how a small hourly loss grows into a large weekly total. A brief discussion invites ideas for how to stop the waste, connecting the mathematical result to everyday conservation action.

periods.teacher_notes: If a live dripping tap is not available, providing a measured amount (for example, 'the container collected 120 ml in one hour') is a valid and equally rich starting point for the calculation work. Students who are comfortable multiplying by 24 and 7 can be stretched to estimate the monthly loss; students who find the multiplication demanding can add the hourly amount repeatedly on a number line. A frequent error is multiplying the hourly loss by 7 directly for the weekly figure, skipping the daily calculation — have students write the daily total first before moving to the week.
materials: Access to a slow-dripping tap (or a teacher-provided sample measurement)
A number line or multiplication chart (for students who need support)

items.section_title: Kilograms and grams — fractions of a kilogram
items.prompt: Four 250 g packets of dal are placed on one side of a pan balance. What should you put on the other side to make the pans balance?

options.label: A
options.text: Five 100 g packets

options.label: B
options.text: One 1 kg packet

options.label: C
options.text: Two 250 g packets

options.label: D
options.text: Two 500 g packets

teacher_guide.expected_answer: One 1 kg packet. Four 250 g packets together weigh 1 kg, so a single 1 kg packet balances them.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Recognise that four 250 g packets equal 1 kg, using the fraction relationship 250 g = ¼ kg.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student halved the number of packets rather than reasoning about total weight; confuses count with mass.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student knows 500 g is related to kg but doubles it rather than recognising that 2×500 g = 1 kg already matches — and has incorrectly equated four 250 g with two 500 g being different from 1 kg.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student is combining two different sub-unit relationships (100 g and 250 g) without checking the total; 5×100 g = 500 g, not 1 kg.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student draw four 250 g boxes and count up 250, 500, 750, 1000; stretch: ask how many 100 g packets would also balance the same pans.

exercise.description: Estimate the weight of 6 bananas, 5 potatoes, 10 tomatoes, 15 onions as less/more than 1 kg; verify using a weighing balance.

items.section_title: Kilograms and grams — fractions of a kilogram
items.prompt: Riya has a bag of rice that weighs ½ kg. She adds another ½ kg of rice. How much does the bag weigh now? Write the weight in kilograms and also in grams.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The bag now weighs 1 kg, which is the same as 1000 g. (½ kg + ½ kg = 1 kg; 500 g + 500 g = 1000 g.)
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use 500 g = ½ kg, so two halves combine to make 1 whole kilogram = 1000 g.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student write 500 g + 500 g = ___ g first, then convert; stretch: ask what the bag weighs if she adds yet another ½ kg, and express that in both kg and g.

exercise.description: Look at pictures: 2×500g=1kg so 500g=½kg; 4×250g=1kg so 250g=¼kg; 10×100g=1kg. Try doing the same with actual packets.

items.section_title: Weighing machines and real-life weight estimation
items.prompt: Which of these objects would you most likely weigh on a bathroom scale?

options.label: A
options.text: A grain of rice

options.label: B
options.text: A medicine tablet

options.label: C
options.text: A newborn baby

options.label: D
options.text: A pinch of salt

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A newborn baby. A bathroom scale measures body weight in kilograms; a newborn is in the kilogram range and is routinely weighed this way.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Match the object's approximate weight range to the scale type that measures that range.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has not connected scale type to weight range; a grain of rice weighs a fraction of a gram and needs a precision scale.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student is not reasoning about the unit scale; a pinch of salt is too light for a bathroom scale to register.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student may be thinking of a pharmacy scale; a medicine tablet is measured in milligrams, far below a bathroom scale's range.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: recall from class which machine was used for babies and which for luggage — let the student match machine to object first; stretch: name one more object suitable for each type of weighing machine.

exercise.description: Lift objects around you; write names of three you can lift easily and estimate their weights.

items.section_title: Measuring capacity — litre, millilitre, and fractions
items.prompt: A jug holds exactly 1 litre. Priya pours in two full 250 ml cups and one full 500 ml bottle. Is the jug now full, not yet full, or overflowing?

options.label: A
options.text: Cannot tell without measuring

options.label: B
options.text: Exactly full — no space left

options.label: C
options.text: Not yet full — some space is left

options.label: D
options.text: Overflowing — too much was poured

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Exactly full. 250 ml + 250 ml + 500 ml = 1000 ml = 1 litre, which fills the jug completely.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add the three amounts: 250 + 250 + 500 = 1000 ml = 1 litre.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may have added only two of the three containers or forgotten that 1000 ml = 1 l.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may have over-estimated one of the amounts or not converted 1000 ml to 1 l correctly.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has not applied the known relationships to compute the total; encourage counting up in steps.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to add the two 250 ml cups first (250 + 250 = 500 ml), then add the 500 ml bottle to 500 ml; stretch: ask what combination of 100 ml, 250 ml, and 500 ml containers could also fill the same jug exactly.

exercise.description: Find bottles/containers that hold less than 1 litre, exactly 1 litre, and more than 1 litre; write their names in the table.

items.section_title: Measuring capacity — litre, millilitre, and fractions
items.prompt:
Look at the number line below. Each mark shows a capacity in ml. Fill in the missing amounts.

The marks go from 0 ml to 1000 ml. Two 250 ml marks and two 500 ml marks are shown; the missing amounts are the ones at the ¼ and ¾ positions.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The missing mark is 500 ml. The sequence is 0, 250, 500, 750, 1000 — each step is 250 ml.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Each step on the line is 250 ml (one quarter of 1000 ml); count up by 250 from the known marks to find the missing one.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student count up by 250 from 0 using fingers or tally marks: 250, 500, 750, 1000; stretch: ask what fraction of 1 litre the missing mark represents and write it as a fraction.

exercise.description: How many 500 ml, 250 ml, 100 ml bottles fill a 1 l bottle? How many 250 ml in ½ l and 750 ml? How many 100 ml in ½ l and 800 ml?

items.section_title: Water use, conservation, and measuring containers
items.prompt: A leaking tap drips 50 ml of water in one hour. How much water does it waste in 4 hours? Write your answer in ml and also say whether it is more or less than ½ litre.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The tap wastes 200 ml in 4 hours (50 × 4 = 200 ml). This is less than ½ litre, because ½ litre = 500 ml and 200 ml < 500 ml.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply the hourly loss by the number of hours: 50 ml × 4 = 200 ml; then compare 200 ml with 500 ml.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student add 50 ml four times in a column (50 + 50 + 50 + 50) rather than multiply; stretch: ask how many more hours the tap would need to drip before the waste reaches exactly ½ litre.

exercise.description: Put a container under a leaking tap for one hour; measure how much water is lost; calculate loss in a day and a week.

items.section_title: Fun at Vegetable Market — comparing weights
items.prompt: Reena says her school bag feels very heavy. Tara says her lunchbox feels light. Which of the following best explains how they know this without using a weighing machine?

options.label: A
options.text: They asked a shopkeeper to tell them.

options.label: B
options.text: They compared the size of the two objects.

options.label: C
options.text: They judged by the effort it took to lift each object.

options.label: D
options.text: They read the weight printed on the objects.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: They judged by the effort it took to lift each object. Effort required to lift is a natural way to estimate and compare weights without a machine.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the physical experience of lifting to judge relative heaviness.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may be thinking of labelled packets; this does not apply to a school bag or lunchbox.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student is confusing size with weight; a large object is not always heavy and a small one is not always light.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student is looking for external authority rather than reasoning from direct experience.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to recall lifting their own bag this morning and describe how it felt; stretch: name one object that is large but light and one that is small but heavy.

exercise.description: Look at pictures of animals and write their names from heaviest to lightest.

items.section_title: Fun at Vegetable Market — comparing weights
items.prompt: A pumpkin weighs 2 kg. The seller cuts it exactly in half and puts one half on the scale. What weight does the scale show? How do you know?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The scale shows 1 kg. Half of 2 kg is 1 kg. Each equal half of the pumpkin weighs the same as the other, so the total splits evenly.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Halving a 2 kg object gives two equal parts of 1 kg each.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to think of 2 kg as 2 big blocks and split them into two equal groups; stretch: if the seller cuts the pumpkin into 4 equal pieces instead, what does each piece weigh?

exercise.description: What do you think will be the weight of the half pumpkin? Write your estimate.

items.section_title: Comparing weights — pan balance and unit matching
items.prompt: One pan of a balance holds a 500 g packet of sugar. The other pan holds two 250 g packets of flour. Which way will the pan balance tilt?

options.label: A
options.text: Cannot tell without knowing the exact weights.

options.label: B
options.text: The flour side goes down.

options.label: C
options.text: The pans stay level.

options.label: D
options.text: The sugar side goes down.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The pans stay level. 500 g on one side equals 250 g + 250 g = 500 g on the other, so both sides weigh the same.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add the weights on each side: 500 g = 250 + 250 g, so both pans are equal and the balance stays level.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may have focused on the single large packet appearing heavier without calculating the total on the other side.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student may have focused on having two packets on one side, assuming more packets means more weight.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has not applied the known gram values already stated in the problem.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student write 250 + 250 = ___ and then compare that number to 500; stretch: describe what you could add to one pan to make it tilt, and say by how much it would be heavier.

exercise.description: How many 250 g packets balance one 500 g packet? Draw packets on the empty pan; complete: 250 g = ___ of 500 g.

items.section_title: Comparing weights — pan balance and unit matching
items.prompt:
Look at these four objects: a pen, a baby, a wooden table, and an eraser. Write each object under the correct heading below.

Headings: Weigh in grams | Weigh in kilograms

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Weigh in grams: pen, eraser. Weigh in kilograms: baby, wooden table. Pens and erasers are small, lightweight objects measured in grams; babies and tables are heavy enough to be measured in kilograms.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Decide which unit fits by judging whether the object's weight is closer to a few grams (very light) or several kilograms (noticeably heavy).
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to first sort into 'very light' and 'quite heavy' by feel or imagination, then assign the unit; stretch: estimate a gram value for the pen and a kilogram value for the baby and explain your reasoning.

exercise.description: Draw arrows to indicate which side the pan balance will tilt for each of the four pictures (a–d).

items.section_title: Comparing weights — pan balance and unit matching
items.prompt: Anu wants to weigh her pet kitten. Which is the best unit and tool to use?

options.label: A
options.text: Grams, using a pan balance with 100 g weights

options.label: B
options.text: Grams, using a small kitchen scale

options.label: C
options.text: Kilograms, using a baby scale

options.label: D
options.text: Kilograms, using a luggage weighing machine

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Kilograms, using a baby scale. A kitten weighs a few kilograms; a baby scale is designed for light living creatures in the kilogram range.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Match the approximate weight of the object (a few kg) to the scale designed for that range.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student is choosing grams, which would give an extremely large and unwieldy number for a kitten; kitchen scales often go up to only 5 kg and are not ideal for a moving animal.
what_each_option_reveals.A: A pan balance with 100 g weights would require many small weights for a kitten in the kg range and is impractical.
what_each_option_reveals.D: A luggage scale is for heavier bags; it may not give accurate readings for a light, small animal.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask what unit we use for a baby's weight and whether a kitten is lighter or heavier than a baby; stretch: explain why a luggage scale would not be a good choice even though it measures in kilograms.

exercise.description: Match objects (baby, eraser, pen, books, table, fridge, etc.) to the units kilogram or grams.

items.section_title: Comparing weights — pan balance and unit matching
items.prompt: A shopkeeper has 1 kg of Besan (chickpea flour). Four customers each want a different box size: 500 g, 250 g, 100 g, and 50 g. How many boxes of each size does the shopkeeper need to pack exactly 1 kg? Write the number for each size.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 500 g box: 2 boxes. 250 g box: 4 boxes. 100 g box: 10 boxes. 50 g box: 20 boxes.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: help the student count up in the box-size steps (e.g. 500, 1000 for the 500 g box) until reaching 1000 g; stretch: ask which box size gives the fewest boxes and which gives the most, and explain why.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Think Q1–Q4 (Boxes of Sweet), p.119
exercise.description: How many boxes of 500 g, 250 g, 100 g, and 50 g each are needed to pack 1 kg Kaju-katli? Write the number for each customer.

items.section_title: Weighing machines and real-life weight estimation
items.prompt: Arjun tries to lift a wooden chair and finds it very hard. Then he lifts a pencil box easily. Which conclusion is most reasonable?

options.label: A
options.text: The chair is heavier than the pencil box.

options.label: B
options.text: The chair is lighter because it is made of wood.

options.label: C
options.text: The pencil box and chair weigh about the same.

options.label: D
options.text: We cannot compare without a weighing machine.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The chair is heavier than the pencil box. The amount of effort needed to lift an object is a reliable way to compare weights when a machine is not available.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Greater lifting effort indicates greater weight; compare effort to judge relative heaviness.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has not connected lifting effort to weight comparison.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student is using material type as a weight indicator rather than the direct experience of lifting effort.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has not applied the lived-experience estimation strategy taught in this section.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to describe what lifting the heaviest book in their bag feels like versus lifting a pencil; stretch: estimate the weight of the chair in kg and explain what you compared it to.

exercise.description: Match objects (cat, elephant, 1-litre bottle, tiger, gas cylinder, pen, leaf, wooden chair) with estimated weight ranges.

items.section_title: Measuring capacity — litre, millilitre, and fractions
items.prompt: Meera has a cough and needs to take 5 ml of syrup three times a day. Is the amount she takes in one day more than, equal to, or less than 20 ml? Write your answer and explain how you know.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Less than 20 ml. She takes 5 ml × 3 times = 15 ml in one day. 15 ml is less than 20 ml.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply the dose by the number of times: 5 ml × 3 = 15 ml; then compare 15 ml with 20 ml.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student draw three 5 ml doses and count up: 5, 10, 15; stretch: ask how many days of medicine are left if the bottle contains 60 ml total.

exercise.description: Find out how much of these liquids are used at a time: eye drops, honey, cough syrup, cooking oil, and one more.

items.section_title: Water use, conservation, and measuring containers
items.prompt: Nisha drinks 2 litres of water each day. Her younger brother drinks 1 litre each day. Together, how much water do they drink in 3 days? Write your answer in litres.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: They drink 9 litres in 3 days. Together they drink 2 + 1 = 3 litres per day; over 3 days that is 3 × 3 = 9 litres.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Find the daily total for both (2 + 1 = 3 l), then multiply by the number of days (3 × 3 = 9 l).
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student draw a table with columns for Day 1, Day 2, Day 3 and add each day's total separately; stretch: ask how many 500 ml bottles they would need to carry their 3-day supply of water.

exercise.description: How many litres of water do you drink daily? How much can a crow drink? How much milk do you drink? How much does an elephant drink?

items.section_title: Water use, conservation, and measuring containers
items.prompt: A household uses about 80 litres of water for one bath/shower. Which activity listed below uses much less water than one shower?

options.label: A
options.text: Filling a large bucket for mopping the floor

options.label: B
options.text: Washing a full load of clothes in a machine

options.label: C
options.text: Watering a large field of crops for one day

options.label: D
options.text: Watering a small pot plant once

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Watering a small pot plant once. A pot plant needs only a small amount of water — far less than 80 litres — while the other activities use comparable or greater amounts.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare each activity's water need against the 80-litre shower benchmark used in the chapter's water-use table.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Watering a large field uses far more water than a shower; the student may not have a sense of agricultural water use.
what_each_option_reveals.B: A washing machine load uses roughly 50–80 litres, comparable to a shower, not much less.
what_each_option_reveals.A: A large mop bucket holds about 10–15 litres — this is less than a shower but the question asks for the activity that uses much less; watering a pot plant uses far less still.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to think about how much water they pour on one small plant at home versus how much fills a bathtub; stretch: rank all four activities from least to most water used and explain your order.

exercise.description: How much water is used in: shower, watering crops, watering plants, washing clothes, and two more activities? Fill the table using given quantities.

items.section_title: Comparing weights — pan balance and unit matching
items.prompt: Each eraser weighs 10 g. How many erasers will weigh the same as a 70 g packet of turmeric powder?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide the target weight by the eraser weight: 70 ÷ 10 = 7, or count up in tens until reaching 70.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to count up by 10 on their fingers: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70 — count the fingers used; stretch: how many erasers would balance a 120 g packet of spices, and what would you call that as a mixed 100 g and 10 g count?

exercise.description: How many erasers (each 10 g) will weigh the same as a 50 g Haldi packet?

items.section_title: Weighing machines and real-life weight estimation
items.prompt: A sack of flour weighs 25 kg. How many 1 kg packets can be filled from this sack?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Since each packet holds exactly 1 kg, the number of packets equals the total kg: 25 kg gives 25 packets.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to imagine putting 1 kg of flour into a bag, sealing it, and repeating — how many times until the sack is empty? Count up to 25; stretch: if each packet is sold for ₹30, what is the total amount earned from the whole sack?

exercise.description: How many 1 kg packets are in 10 kg, 20 kg, 50 kg, and 25 kg? Write the answers.

items.section_title: Measuring capacity — litre, millilitre, and fractions
items.prompt: A shopkeeper has 1 litre of rose water. A customer wants it packed in 200 ml bottles. How many bottles does the shopkeeper need?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Convert 1 litre to 1000 ml, then count how many 200 ml portions fit: 200, 400, 600, 800, 1000 — five steps.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to count up in steps of 200 on a number line from 0 to 1000 and count the steps; stretch: if the shopkeeper also has 500 ml of the same rose water and packs it in 100 ml bottles, how many more bottles are needed in total?

exercise.description: Mr Krishna has 1 l perfumed oil; how many bottles of 500 ml, 200 ml, 100 ml, and 50 ml does each customer get?
